newsitem.title: USA: Cancer panel likely to recommend mammograms in 40s.
newsitem.headline: Cancer panel likely to recommend mammograms in 40s.

text.p: Hoping to end four years of rising controversy, advisers to the National Cancer Institute Thursday will recommend that women in their forties get regular mammograms, activists and a panel member said Wednesday.

"The last I heard, they were making recommendations that women in their 40s have a mammogram every one or two years," said Susan Braun, president of the Dallas-based Susan B. Komen Breast Cancer Foundation. Several other activists and health officials who track the controversy this week reported a similar understanding.

Zora Brown, a member of the National Cancer Advisory Board, in a telephone interview confirmed the activists' account, with a slight variant. Brown said the panel will recommend that most women at "normal" risk have the breast cancer screening every other year, but women at "high risk" should have it annually.

"I absolutely believe there is a benefit in the 40s," she said, adding that she hopes the attention can now switch to making sure that women, including those with little or no health insurance, get access to good medical treatment.
National Cancer Institute Director Dr. Richard Klausner was likely to endorse the advisory panel's recommendations.
There has been no question that mammograms save lives among women over 50. And there is widespread opinion that women under 40 don't need mammograms, unless they are at special genetic risk.
The picture for 40-year-olds has been less clear, clouded partly by limited data and partly by all the politics and publicity that have come into play in the past few months.

Although breast cancer is the leading cause of death for U.S. women in their 40s, it is not that common in that age group. About four out of five of 182,000 breast cancers diagnosed in a typical year are in women over 50, with the risk increasing steadily with age.

Studies of women in their 40s have produced mixed results -- although proponents of screening tend to cite the more positive reports. According to a "meta-analysis" combining the major studies for the advisory group, the best working estimate is that mammograms could decrease the breast cancer death rate for women in their 40s by about 17 percent.
Several other members of the National Cancer Advisory Board refused to publicly discuss the panel's conclusiosn before the official announcement Thursday morning.

University of Maryland cancer expert Kay Dickersin declined to discuss the report but noted, "The press has put tremendous pressure on the National Cancer Institute to say something different from what the consensus panel said."
Dickersin was referring to a consensus panel of outside experts, charged with making recommendations reviewing the latest worldwide data on mammograms for women in their 40s.

Instead of coming down firmly for or against mammograms in that age group, the consensus conference in January said women should make up their own minds in consultation with their doctors. That conclusion immediate turned a simmering controvery into a firestorm.

Angry women's health advocates clamoured for a clear answer. Politicians got into the picture, holding congressional hearings and passing resolutions directed at the NCI. Newspapers gave the mammogram story front-page treatment.

Until 1993, the NCI had recommended regular mammograms for women in their 40s, as did the American Cancer Society. But studies did not show a clear life-saving benefit for women under 50, and the NCI then dropped the recommendation.

The cancer society and other medical groups continued to recommend mammograms for women in their 40s. In its most recent recommendations, the American Cancer Society said women in their 40s should get the screening every year."
